concept.name: Low-volatility factor
concept.definition: A factor built on the empirical finding that low-beta and low-volatility stocks have historically earned higher risk-adjusted returns than the CAPM predicts - the security market line is empirically too flat - formalized by Frazzini and Pedersen as the Betting Against Beta (BAB) factor, which goes long leveraged low-beta assets and short de-leveraged high-beta assets.
concept.intuition: Risky stocks don't pay as much per unit of risk as theory says they should, so tilting toward calm stocks has historically improved Sharpe ratios.
concept.mechanics: Stocks are ranked by estimated beta (or volatility); the long side holds low-beta names (scaled up toward comparable risk) and the short side holds high-beta names (scaled down). Frazzini and Pedersen attribute the effect to leverage constraints: investors unable or unwilling to lever instead overweight high-beta securities, depressing their risk-adjusted returns.
concept.formula: BAB return = (1/beta_L)(r_L - r_f) - (1/beta_H)(r_H - r_f), where r_L, r_H are returns of low- and high-beta portfolios and beta_L, beta_H their betas.
concept.failure_modes: The factor underperforms sharply when high-beta stocks rally (strong bull rebounds), is exposed to crowding and valuation risk in the low-vol sleeve, and can load heavily on interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities, adding hidden rate risk.
concept.misconceptions: Low volatility is not low absolute risk in all senses: low-beta portfolios still fall in market crashes (they just fall less), and the anomaly concerns risk-adjusted, not raw, returns.
concept.example: Sorting U.S. stocks by beta and holding the lowest-beta decile against the highest, with each side scaled to beta 1, reproduces the BAB factor; Frazzini and Pedersen document the flat security market line in 18 of 19 international equity markets.

citations.source: AQR Capital Management, Frazzini and Pedersen, Betting Against Beta (Journal of Financial Economics)
